angle: angle 1 · a place and a time
title: Saturday at the Mall in 1984: The America We Lost

scenes.text: It's a Saturday morning in nineteen eighty-four. You've got twenty dollars from your paper route in your pocket, your hair is feathered just right, and your mom is dropping you and your friends off at the main entrance. She'll pick you up at four, by the fountain. You walk through the glass doors, and there it is. The mall.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY, 1984

scenes.text: In the nineteen eighties, the shopping mall was the center of American life, especially for teenagers. It was where you shopped, ate, played video games, saw movies, met friends and maybe met someone special. In those years, America built new malls at a remarkable pace, and by the end of the decade there were thousands of them.
scenes.caption: THE CENTER OF AMERICAN LIFE

scenes.text: So let's spend a Saturday at the mall in nineteen eighty-four. From opening time to closing time. The stores, the food court, the arcade, the music and the people. If you were there, you might just hear the fountain splashing and smell the Cinnabon.
scenes.caption: FROM OPENING TO CLOSING

scenes.text: The mall had been growing for decades. The first fully enclosed mall, Southdale Center in Edina, Minnesota, had opened in nineteen fifty-six. Through the sixties and seventies, malls spread to every suburb in the country. By the eighties, they had pulled the shoppers away from downtown Main Streets almost everywhere. The mall had become the new Main Street.
scenes.caption: THE NEW MAIN STREET

scenes.text: At ten o'clock, the metal gates rolled up on hundreds of storefronts. The mall was clean and quiet. The first people inside were the mall walkers, older men and women in tracksuits and white sneakers, walking laps in the air conditioning. Many malls opened early just for them.
scenes.caption: THE MALL WALKERS

scenes.text: The malls of the eighties were bright and modern, with skylights, glass elevators, brass railings, potted palm trees and huge fountains. Some had ice skating rinks, carousels or even small amusement parks. Shoppers threw coins into the fountains and made wishes. Some malls collected thousands of dollars a year from them for charity.
scenes.caption: THE FOUNTAIN

scenes.text: At each end of the mall stood the anchor stores, the big department stores. Sears, J.C. Penney, Montgomery Ward, Macy's or a regional chain like Hudson's, Marshall Field's or Bullock's. Parents shopped there for clothes, appliances and towels. Kids went there to use the restroom and look at the electronics.
scenes.caption: THE ANCHOR STORES

scenes.text: Getting there was half the adventure. Teenagers without a license begged rides from parents or older siblings. In some towns, a city bus stopped right at the mall entrance. Kids rode their bikes for miles and locked them to the rack outside Sears. And once you got your license, driving your friends to the mall on Saturday was the whole point of having a car.
scenes.caption: GETTING THERE

scenes.text: In between were the smaller stores, and for teenagers, they were the real attraction. There was the record store, like Sam Goody or Camelot Music, with racks of vinyl albums and cassette tapes. In nineteen eighty-four, everyone was buying Michael Jackson's Thriller, Prince's Purple Rain, Bruce Springsteen's Born in the U.S.A. and Madonna.
scenes.caption: SAM GOODY

scenes.text: There was the bookstore, B. Dalton or Waldenbooks, where kids read comic books and magazines without buying them until a clerk shooed them away. There was Radio Shack, with its batteries, walkie-talkies and the new TRS-80 computer. And there was Spencer Gifts, with its black lights, lava lamps, gag gifts and posters.
scenes.caption: WALDENBOOKS AND RADIO SHACK

scenes.text: For clothes, teenagers went to The Limited, Chess King, Merry-Go-Round, County Seat and The Gap. The fashion of eighty-four meant parachute pants, Members Only jackets, Swatch watches, jelly bracelets, leg warmers and acid-wash jeans. Girls wore big bangs held up with Aqua Net hairspray. Boys wore Izod shirts with the collar popped up.
scenes.caption: MEMBERS ONLY

scenes.text: Then there was the shoe store. Nike Air Jordans wouldn't arrive until the following year, but in nineteen eighty-four, kids wanted Nike, Reebok, Converse high-tops and Vans. Girls wanted Keds and jelly shoes. And at the Foot Locker, the clerks wore referee shirts and measured your feet with a metal Brannock device, just like the shoe stores of their parents' day.
scenes.caption: THE REFEREE SHIRTS

scenes.text: And there was the toy store, KB Toys or Kay-Bee, packed with He-Man figures, Transformers, which arrived that very year, Care Bears, Strawberry Shortcake and Rubik's Cubes. And everyone was looking for a Cabbage Patch Kid. The year before, at Christmas of nineteen eighty-three, parents had literally fought in stores to get one.
scenes.caption: CABBAGE PATCH KIDS

scenes.text: And there was the electronics store, where crowds gathered around the newest gadgets. The Sony Walkman, which let you carry your music anywhere. Boom boxes the size of suitcases. Atari and ColecoVision game consoles. And at the very end of January nineteen eighty-four, Apple introduced the Macintosh computer, with a famous television ad during the Super Bowl.
scenes.caption: THE NEWEST GADGETS

scenes.text: For many kids, the best part of the mall was the arcade. Aladdin's Castle, Tilt, or Time Out. Dark rooms full of flashing lights and electronic sounds, where every game cost a quarter. The change machine on the wall turned your dollar bills into a stack of quarters, and they disappeared fast.
scenes.caption: A QUARTER A GAME

scenes.text: The games of nineteen eighty-four were legends. Pac-Man, Ms. Pac-Man, Donkey Kong, Galaga, Centipede, Frogger and Dragon's Lair. The best players drew a crowd. They put their initials on the high score screen. And a kid who could play Galaga for an hour on one quarter was famous at school on Monday.
scenes.caption: PAC-MAN

scenes.text: Parents left younger kids at the arcade while they shopped. Older kids hung out there for hours. It was loud, dark and a little bit rough around the edges, and that was exactly why teenagers loved it.
scenes.caption: LOUD AND DARK

scenes.text: Next door, there might be a photo booth. Four pictures for a dollar, printed in a strip a few minutes later. Friends crammed into the tiny booth, made silly faces, and split the strip. Many people still have those little strips tucked into old yearbooks and shoeboxes, the only photos they have of that afternoon.
scenes.caption: FOUR PICTURES FOR A DOLLAR

scenes.text: By noon, everyone was hungry, and everyone headed to the food court. The food court was a new idea in the seventies and eighties. A big open area full of tables, surrounded by counters selling every kind of fast food. Pizza, tacos, Chinese food, hot dogs and hamburgers, all in one place.
scenes.caption: THE FOOD COURT

scenes.text: There was Orange Julius, with its frothy orange drink. Hot Dog on a Stick, where the employees wore those famous striped uniforms and tall hats. Sbarro for pizza. Chick-fil-A, which started in a mall in Atlanta. And the Great American Cookie Company, with giant cookies, and the smell of fresh pretzels drifting through the whole mall.
scenes.caption: ORANGE JULIUS

scenes.text: Teenagers sat at the food court for hours, nursing one soda. They gossiped, flirted, made plans, and watched everyone go by. For a generation of kids, the food court was what the soda fountain had been to their parents. The place where everyone met.
scenes.caption: WHERE EVERYONE MET

scenes.text: And the sweet smells were everywhere. Cinnabon opened its first store in a mall near Seattle in nineteen eighty-five, and the smell of its cinnamon rolls would soon fill malls across the country. There were candy stores selling jelly beans by the pound, made famous by President Reagan, who kept a jar of them on his desk.
scenes.caption: JELLY BEANS

scenes.text: Hanging out at the mall was a national pastime. Parents felt it was safe. It was indoors, there were security guards, and nothing bad was supposed to happen at the mall. So kids were dropped off for whole afternoons. They walked laps, window shopped, and went nowhere in particular.
scenes.caption: HANGING OUT

scenes.text: Kids called them mall rats. They had no money to spend, but they knew every store, every clerk and every bench. They knew which store had the cutest employees and which security guard would kick you out for sitting on the fountain. The mall was their neighborhood.
scenes.caption: MALL RATS

scenes.text: Teenagers had their first jobs at the mall too. Scooping ice cream, folding sweaters at the Gap, selling shoes at Foot Locker or working the counter at Hot Dog on a Stick. A sixteen-year-old in nineteen eighty-four earned the minimum wage of three thirty-five an hour. And you got an employee discount.
scenes.caption: $3.35 AN HOUR

scenes.text: And the mall had its own soundtrack. Soft music played from speakers in the ceiling, easy-listening versions of popular songs. Each store played its own music too, so walking down the corridor meant hearing a dozen songs at once. The splash of the fountain. The beep of the cash registers. The squeak of sneakers on the shiny tile floor.
scenes.caption: THE SOUNDTRACK

scenes.text: In the afternoon, there was a movie. Many malls had a movie theater with two to six screens. In the summer of nineteen eighty-four, it might have been Ghostbusters, Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, Gremlins or The Karate Kid. Tickets cost about three dollars and fifty cents.
scenes.caption: GHOSTBUSTERS

scenes.text: Families came in the afternoon too. Mothers with strollers. Fathers looking at power tools at Sears. Grandparents resting on the benches. Little kids riding the coin-operated horses and rocket ships. On weekends, there might be a car show in the center court, a craft fair, or a school choir singing.
scenes.caption: THE WHOLE FAMILY

scenes.text: And at Christmas, the mall was magical. Giant decorations hung from the ceiling. Santa sat on a throne in the center court, and the line to see him stretched for an hour. Shoppers carried armloads of bags. And the sound of carols mixed with the splashing of the fountain.
scenes.caption: CHRISTMAS AT THE MALL

scenes.text: By four o'clock, your feet hurt, your money was gone, and your mom was waiting by the fountain. You had a bag from the record store with one cassette in it, a Swatch you'd been saving for, and a story about who you saw at the food court. It had been a great day.
scenes.caption: YOUR MONEY WAS GONE

scenes.text: At nine o'clock, the stores closed. The gates rolled down. The lights dimmed. The cleaning crews came out with their floor polishers. And in the empty parking lot, the last cars pulled away under the tall orange lights. Tomorrow, it would all start again.
scenes.caption: THE GATES ROLLED DOWN

scenes.text: So what happened to the mall? In the nineties and two thousands, things began to change. Big-box stores like Walmart and Target offered lower prices. Outlet malls and strip centers grew. Then came online shopping. Amazon, founded in nineteen ninety-four, made it possible to buy almost anything without leaving home.
scenes.caption: ONLINE SHOPPING

scenes.text: The anchor stores began to close. Sears, J.C. Penney and Macy's shut hundreds of locations. When an anchor closed, the smaller stores lost their customers too. Many malls fell into decline. Today, hundreds of American malls are dead or dying, with empty storefronts, dry fountains and silent food courts.
scenes.caption: DEAD MALLS

scenes.text: Some malls have been torn down and replaced with apartments, offices or outdoor shopping centers. Some have become churches, schools or medical centers. Photographers travel the country taking pictures of abandoned malls, and people watch videos of them online, feeling a strange nostalgia for a place that once felt so ordinary.
scenes.caption: A STRANGE NOSTALGIA

scenes.text: What did we lose? Not just stores. We lost a place where the whole community gathered, under one roof, on a Saturday afternoon. Teenagers, parents, grandparents and toddlers, all in the same place at the same time. Today, we mostly shop alone, on our phones.
scenes.caption: UNDER ONE ROOF

scenes.text: If you were a teenager in nineteen eighty-four, you remember. The Orange Julius. The arcade. The record store. The fountain full of pennies. Your friends, your feathered hair and your Walkman. The mall was your world, and for a few years, it was everybody's.
scenes.caption: IT WAS YOUR WORLD

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What was the name of your mall? What was your favorite store, and what did you always eat at the food court? Did you have a job at the mall? We read every comment. Next time, we're looking at what it meant to turn thirty in nineteen seventy-nine. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS YOUR MALL?
